questions.question_text: Under Wis. Stat. s. 452.132, who has the duty to supervise a firm's licensees?
questions.correct_answer: The firm, which delegates the duty to a supervising broker
distractors: Each individual salesperson, for their own conduct
The DSPS licensing coordinator
The firm's office manager
questions.explanation: The supervision duty sits with the firm (Wis. Stat. s. 452.132 (1)). Under s. 452.132 (5) (a) a licensed broker business entity must delegate it in writing to a supervising broker who is a licensed individual broker; under (5) (b) a firm that is not a business entity is itself deemed the supervising broker absent a delegation. Wisconsin's statutory term is 'supervising broker,' not 'designated broker.'

questions.question_text: A salesperson places a misleading ad without the firm's knowledge. Under Wis. Stat. s. 452.12 (3), when is the firm responsible?
questions.correct_answer: Only to the extent the firm failed to comply with its s. 452.132 supervision duties
distractors: Always — a firm is automatically liable for its licensees' conduct
Only if the supervising broker personally approved the ad
Never — each licensee is solely responsible for their own ads
questions.explanation: A firm is responsible for brokerage services provided on its behalf by an associated licensee 'only to the extent that the firm fails to comply with s. 452.132' (Wis. Stat. s. 452.12 (3)). 2015 Wisconsin Act 258 deliberately replaced blanket vicarious liability with this supervision-based standard. The salesperson remains liable for their own violation.

questions.question_text: Which duty does NOT fall under the designated broker's supervisory responsibilities?
distractors: Maintaining proper trust accounts
Ensuring advertising compliance
Overseeing licensee conduct
questions.explanation: The supervising broker's role is supervision, trust account integrity, and advertising compliance. Inspecting the property under REEB 24.07 (1) is a duty of the licensee working the transaction, not a supervisory function.

questions.question_text: How many supervising brokers may a Wisconsin firm have?
questions.correct_answer: One or more — a firm may delegate the duty to multiple supervising brokers
distractors: Exactly one, in every case
One for every 10 salespersons
None, for firms with fewer than 5 agents
questions.explanation: A firm may delegate the supervision duty to more than one supervising broker (Wis. Stat. s. 452.132 (5) (d)). A licensed broker business entity must make at least one written delegation under (5) (a); a firm that is not a business entity is deemed its own supervising broker under (5) (b) if it makes none.

questions.question_text: A firm's real estate trust account is found to be short by $2,000. Whose obligation was breached?
questions.correct_answer: The firm's — REEB 18 places trust account duties on the firm
distractors: The salesperson's who last made a deposit
The firm's accountant or bookkeeper's
DSPS's, which monitors all trust account deposits
questions.explanation: The deposit, custody, and bookkeeping duties sit with the firm, and trust account records are part of the supervising broker's pre-closing review (Wis. Admin. Code REEB 18.031 and 18.13; Wis. Stat. s. 452.132 (4) (a) 2.). Under s. 452.13 (2) (b) 3. the firm must authorize DSPS and the Department of Administration to examine and audit the account.

questions.question_text: A Wisconsin salesperson receives a $5,000 earnest money check. What must they do?
questions.correct_answer: Turn it over to the broker promptly
distractors: Deposit it in their personal bank account
Hold it until closing day
Give it directly to the seller
questions.explanation: A licensee who receives real estate trust funds must promptly submit them to the firm (Wis. Admin. Code REEB 18.031 (2)). The firm then deposits them in a real estate trust account within 48 hours of receipt under REEB 18.031 (1).

questions.question_text: Can a Wisconsin salesperson operate independently without a broker?
questions.correct_answer: No, salespersons must be associated with a licensed broker
distractors: Yes, after 5 years of experience
Yes, with REEB special approval
Yes, for transactions under $100,000
questions.explanation: Wisconsin salespersons cannot practice independently. They must be supervised by and associated with a licensed broker or firm. The broker is responsible for the salesperson's professional conduct.

questions.question_text: A salesperson wants to move from one firm to another. What does Wis. Stat. s. 452.30 require?
questions.correct_answer: Notice to DSPS on the prescribed form with the transfer fee, before providing services for the new firm
distractors: A 30-day waiting period between firms
Advance approval of the transfer by REEB
Nothing beyond signing on with the new firm
questions.explanation: A licensee may not provide brokerage services on a firm's behalf unless they are associated with the firm AND have notified the department (Wis. Stat. s. 452.30 (1)). Subs. (3) and (2) (b) require notice on the department's form with the s. 440.05 (7) transfer fee. Separately, s. 452.30 (4) gives both the licensee and the terminating firm 10 days to file notice that the association ended.

questions.question_text: A salesperson's broker has their license suspended. What happens to the salesperson's ability to practice?
questions.correct_answer: They cannot practice until associated with another broker
distractors: They can continue practicing independently
Their license is automatically suspended too
DSPS assigns them a temporary broker
questions.explanation: Since salespersons must work under a licensed broker, if their broker's license is suspended, the salesperson cannot practice until they associate with another licensed broker or firm.

questions.question_text: How did 2015 Wisconsin Act 258 change a firm's responsibility for its licensees' conduct?
questions.correct_answer: It limited the firm's responsibility to its own failure to supervise under s. 452.132
distractors: It made firms strictly liable for everything a licensee does
It moved responsibility entirely onto the individual licensee
It made DSPS responsible for supervising licensee conduct
questions.explanation: A firm is responsible for brokerage services provided by an associated licensee only to the extent the firm failed to comply with s. 452.132 (Wis. Stat. s. 452.12 (3), as rewritten by Act 258). Section 452.132 (4) (b) further limits the supervising broker's pre-closing review to confirming the s. 452.135 disclosures were provided, confirming an applicable approved form was used with its blanks filled consistently with the form's structure, and communicating errors apparent on the face of the document.

questions.question_text: Under Wis. Stat. s. 452.40 and REEB 16, what may a Wisconsin licensee do with an approved WB form?
questions.correct_answer: Fill in blanks and modify printed provisions at a party's instruction
distractors: Only fill in blanks — never alter printed text
Draft a replacement form from scratch
Give the party a legal opinion on the form's effect
questions.explanation: To 'use a form' means completing it by filling in blanks OR modifying printed provisions on the form at a party's instruction (Wis. Stat. s. 452.40 (1) (a); REEB 16.02 (5) repeats the definition). REEB 16.06 (3) lets a licensee cross out provisions so long as the deleted text remains legible. What s. 452.40 (2) forbids is advice on legal rights or obligations, the legal effect of a contract, or the state of title.

questions.question_text: A buyer asks their agent to add a custom clause to the WB-11. What may the agent do?
questions.correct_answer: Fill in the blank lines provided, or attach an addendum prepared by the firm or an attorney
distractors: Nothing — only an attorney may alter a WB form in any way
Refuse, because custom clauses are never permitted
Ask REEB to approve the clause before using it
questions.explanation: A pre-prepared addendum may be prepared by the firm or by an attorney where it relates to the form's blanks or alters optional provisions (REEB 16.06 (4) (a)). Only an addendum that supplants or alters the form's printed provisions must be attorney-drafted, under REEB 16.06 (5) (a). REEB 16.06 (8) requires the licensee to use forms and prepare addenda so as to adequately accomplish the party's contractual instruction.

questions.question_text: A client asks their agent to explain what a contract term legally means. The agent should:
questions.correct_answer: Refer the client to an attorney for legal advice
distractors: Explain the legal meaning to the best of their ability
Look up the answer in the REEB handbook
Ask their broker for the legal interpretation
questions.explanation: A licensee may not give advice or opinions on the legal rights or obligations of parties, the legal effect of a specific contract or conveyance, or the state of title (Wis. Stat. s. 452.40 (2); REEB 16.05 (1)). The licensee should refer the legal question to an attorney — and under REEB 24.06 (2) may never discourage anyone from retaining one.

questions.question_text: Which action by a Wisconsin licensee would be the unauthorized practice of law?
questions.correct_answer: Telling the parties what a contract provision legally means for their rights
distractors: Crossing out a printed provision at a party's instruction
Filling in the blank fields on a WB-11
Attaching an attorney-drafted addendum to a WB form
questions.explanation: The line falls at advice or opinions on legal rights or obligations, the legal effect of a specific contract or conveyance, or the state of title (Wis. Stat. s. 452.40 (2)). That same subsection expressly permits a general explanation of an approved form's provisions. Crossing out provisions is allowed by REEB 16.06 (3), and modifying printed provisions is part of the statutory definition of 'use a form.'

questions.question_text: Is filling in the blanks on a REEB-approved form considered legal advice?
questions.correct_answer: No, it is not considered legal advice
distractors: Yes, only attorneys should fill in forms
Yes, but REEB grants an exception to licensees
It depends on the complexity of the transaction
questions.explanation: A firm and its licensees may use board-approved forms in real estate practice, and a general explanation of a form's provisions is expressly permitted when completing it or delivering it for acceptance (Wis. Stat. s. 452.40 (1) (b), (2)). Section 452.132 (4) also provides that a supervising broker's review is not the provision of legal advice.
